_note: Prototype thresholds. Bands: value inside 'green' = green, inside 'yellow' = yellow, otherwise red. Full rationale and citations in docs/RESEARCH.md section 7. Not medical advice.

indicators.label: Resting heart rate
indicators.how: Sit still for 5 minutes, then read your wearable or count your wrist pulse for 30 seconds and double it.
indicators.why: Weightlessness changes how the heart and blood vessels work and can even make the heart rounder. Heart-rate trends show how your cardiovascular system is adapting.

action.yellow: Rest, drink water, and recheck in 1 hour. If you feel palpitations or dizziness, log them.
action.red: Stop activity. Notify the crew medical officer and send a report to the flight surgeon (expect up to a 20-minute one-way delay).

indicators.label: Blood pressure (systolic)
indicators.how: Use the arm cuff seated, arm at heart level, after 5 minutes of rest.
indicators.why: Fluid shifts alter blood pressure control. Low pressure raises the chance of fainting during gravity transitions such as landing.

action.yellow: Recheck after 10 minutes of rest. Before a landing, follow fluid-loading and compression-garment procedures.
action.red: Notify the crew medical officer and flight surgeon. If low and dizzy, lie down with legs raised.

indicators.label: Blood pressure (diastolic)
indicators.how: Recorded at the same time as systolic pressure.
indicators.why: Part of the full blood pressure picture for cardiovascular adaptation.

action.yellow: Recheck after rest; review salt and fluid intake.
action.red: Notify the crew medical officer and flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Blood oxygen (SpO₂)
indicators.how: Clip the pulse oximeter on a warm finger and hold still for 30 seconds.
indicators.why: Future habitats may run at lower pressure to make spacewalks safer, which raises the risk of mild hypoxia: headache, confusion, vision problems and poor sleep.

action.yellow: Rest and recheck in 15 minutes. Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ readings.
action.red: Use supplemental oxygen per procedure and notify the crew medical officer immediately.

indicators.label: Blood glucose (fasting)
indicators.how: Fingerstick glucometer in the morning, before eating.
indicators.why: Diet changes, menu fatigue, stress and inactivity affect metabolism. Nutrition is essential for health and performance on long missions.

action.yellow: If low: eat a snack with fast carbs and recheck in 15 minutes. If high: review meals and exercise.
action.red: Notify the crew medical officer and flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Body temperature
indicators.how: Use the forehead or ear thermometer, at rest.
indicators.why: Spaceflight stress can weaken immunity and reactivate dormant viruses (cold sores, shingles), and microbes can be more virulent in space. Note: on long missions resting core temperature rises about 1 °C over the first 2.5 months (Stahn et al. 2017), so compare with your own in-flight trend. A new rise above your usual, especially with symptoms, matters most.

action.yellow: Rest, hydrate, recheck in 2 hours, and log any rash, cold sore or sore throat.
action.red: Limit close contact with crewmates and notify the crew medical officer and flight surgeon.

indicators.label: Sleep
indicators.how: Read from your wrist sensor, or log when you fell asleep and woke up.
indicators.why: ISS crews see 16 sunrises a day. Irregular light, work overload and noise disrupt sleep, which hurts performance and health.

action.yellow: Use the sleep-mode lighting, avoid caffeine in the afternoon, and keep a fixed sleep window.
action.red: Report fatigue to the commander before safety-critical tasks and ask for a schedule adjustment.

indicators.label: Mood (1–10)
indicators.how: Rate how you feel today from 1 (very low) to 10 (great). Honest answers matter more than high ones.
indicators.why: Isolation, confinement and distance from Earth raise the risk of anxiety and depression, which affect sleep, morale and decisions.

action.yellow: Try a self-care activity: journaling, tending plants, looking out a window, or a recorded message from family.
action.red: Request a private conference with ground support. You don't have to handle this alone.

indicators.label: Exercise
indicators.how: Logged automatically from the exercise device, or enter resistance and aerobic minutes.
indicators.why: Without gravity, bones lose 1–1.5% of density per month and strength and aerobic fitness drop 10–12% on average. ISS crews exercise 1.5 hours a day to fight this.

action.yellow: Add a resistance session today to reach 90 minutes.
action.red: You're well below the countermeasure target. Schedule exercise before other optional tasks.

indicators.label: Water intake
indicators.how: Log each drink bag, or read from the water dispenser.
indicators.why: Dehydration plus calcium released from shrinking bones raises kidney stone risk. Good hydration also helps prevent fainting at landing.

action.yellow: Drink another 500 mL over the next few hours.
action.red: Rehydrate now and watch for flank pain or dark urine.

indicators.label: Cumulative radiation dose
indicators.how: Read automatically from your personal dosimeter. You cannot see or feel radiation.
indicators.why: Radiation raises cancer risk and can affect the brain, heart and eyes. NASA's career limit is 600 mSv. Daily dose: ~0.5 mSv on the ISS, 1.84 in Mars transit, 1.37 on the Moon, 0.64 on Mars.

action.yellow: Over 50% of the career limit. Minimize time in low-shielding areas and review the EVA plan with the flight surgeon.
action.red: Over 80% of the career limit. The flight surgeon must review all further exposure. During a solar storm alert, go to the shielded shelter.

indicators.label: Body mass
indicators.how: Use the body mass measuring device. Scales don't work in weightlessness, so on the ISS it uses springs and Newton's second law.
indicators.why: Menu fatigue, nausea and stress can make crews eat less. Over months that shows up as weight loss, which hurts strength, bone and performance.

action.yellow: More than 3% change from your baseline. Eat full rations and log meals; tell the CMO if it continues.
action.red: More than 6% change from your baseline. Notify the CMO and flight surgeon for a nutrition review.
